extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; design patent applicants, agents, and attorneys preparing or prosecuting U.S. design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and examining drawings/photographs that constitute the entire visual disclosure of a U.S. design patent application, including required views, shading, broken-line usage, photographs/color rules, amendment/replacement procedures, and avoiding new matter. Intended to ensure drawings are clear, complete, and legally sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 112 and relevant regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and sufficiency of views
rubrics_metrics.description: The design must be represented by a drawing that complies with § 1.84 and must contain a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Views should disclose the complete appearance of the claimed design and may include front, rear, top, bottom and sides. Perspective views are suggested for three-dimensional designs and, if clearly understood, may obviate the need to illustrate the same surfaces in other views. Views that are merely duplicative or flat and include no surface ornamentation may be omitted if the specification explicitly states so (e.g., one side shown and the other stated as identical or mirror image; bottom may be omitted if stated flat and unornamented). If inconsistencies among views make the overall appearance unclear, the examiner should object and, if so severe, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs). Sectional views solely showing internal construction or functional features are unnecessary and may be objected to; sectional views may be included only when exterior contour is not apparent and no internal construction is attempted. When sectional views are added during prosecution, check for antecedent basis for hatching per 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate and adequate surface shading should be used to show the character or contour of the surfaces represented; surface shading is not required by 37 CFR 1.152 but may be necessary in particular cases to show 3‑D aspects and to distinguish open and solid areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface shading is important for depicting plane, concave, convex, raised, and depressed surfaces and to distinguish open vs closed areas. Lack of appropriate surface shading in the drawing as filed may render the design nonenabling and indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs). Addition of surface shading after filing may constitute new matter. Solid black surface shading is not permitted except to represent the color black or color contrast. Oblique line shading must be used to show transparent, translucent, and highly polished or reflective surfaces (e.g., mirror). Contrast in materials may be shown by using line shading in one area and stippling in another to broadly cover contrasting surfaces without limiting to specific colors. Use form paragraph 15.49 to notify applicant that surface shading is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and description of broken lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines may be used to show visible environmental structure or to define bounds of the claim but may not be used to show hidden planes/surfaces or to indicate that a portion is of less importance in the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed subject matter (environment) may be shown in broken lines and must be described as forming no part of the claimed design or of a specified embodiment. A broken-line boundary may be used to define the bounds of a claimed design, but any broken-line boundary other than a straight broken line may constitute new matter. Broken lines must not be used to show hidden planes and surfaces that cannot be seen through opaque materials. Broken lines should not intrude upon or cross the showing of the claimed design and should not be heavier than full lines. If broken lines cross over full lines, the specification must explicitly identify their purpose (e.g., distinguishing broken-line bounds from broken-line environment), and when broken-line environment obscures the claimed design a separate figure showing the broken lines must be included. Use the prescribed statement to describe broken lines in the specification: “The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.” See also form paragraphs 15.50–15.50.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed design must be shown in full (solid) lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The ornamental design being claimed must be shown in solid lines in the drawing; dotted lines for the purpose of indicating unimportant or immaterial features are not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no portions of a claimed design that are immaterial or unimportant. Dotted/broken lines cannot be used to indicate that part of a claimed design is unimportant. Use form paragraph 15.50 to notify applicants where claimed subject matter is not shown in full lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectional views and internal-construction depictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sectional views presented solely to show internal construction or functional/mechanical features are unnecessary and may lead to confusion as to the scope of the claimed design and should be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 112 (second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sectional views may be included only where the exact contour or configuration of the exterior surface of a claimed design is not apparent from the views and no attempt is made to illustrate internal construction. If sectional hatching is added during prosecution, determine whether there is antecedent basis in the original disclosure for the material shown in hatching (37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) and MPEP § 608.02). See cited authorities (Ex parte Tucker; Ex parte Kohler; Ex parte Lohman) for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface treatment disclosure rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface treatment (shape/configuration plus indicia, contrasting color or materials, graphic representations, or other ornamentation applied to the article) must be applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture; surface treatment per se is not proper subject matter for a design patent under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface treatment may be shown in full lines (claimed) or broken lines (unclaimed) and is prima facie evidence that the inventor considered it integral to the claimed design. An amendment canceling two-dimensional surface treatment or reducing it to broken lines is permissible if the underlying configuration without the surface treatment is apparent in the original disclosure; removal of three-dimensional surface treatment that is integral to configuration (e.g., beading, grooves, ribs) will introduce prohibited new matter. Guidelines for computer-generated icons apply equally to all types of surface treatment. See MPEP § 1504.01 and § 1504.04 for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs and color-drawing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are normally required in black ink on white paper; photographs are acceptable only when the invention cannot be illustrated in an ink drawing or is shown more clearly in a photograph. Color photographs/drawings have special petition requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84(b) and must be limited to the design claimed for the article (must not disclose environmental structure). Only one set of black-and-white photographs is required. Color photographs and color drawings may be submitted only with a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2); a grantable petition must: explain that color is integral to the claimed design, include the fee (37 CFR 1.17(h)), include three sets of the color photos/drawings, and include an amendment to the specification inserting a statement that the file contains at least one drawing/photograph executed in color. If informal color photos/drawings are filed for filing-date purposes, applicant must later submit the petition/fee/sets/statements to treat them as formal. Photographs and ink drawings must not be combined as the formal visual disclosure in one application. If photographs are not of sufficient quality to reproduce all details, objections will be raised and no patent will be issued until acceptable photographs are submitted and approved. If color photographs/drawings are filed originally, color is considered an integral part of the claimed design; omission of color later may be permitted only if underlying configuration without color is clear from the application (see In re Daniels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal color submissions accepted for filing date only
rubrics_metrics.description: For filing-date purposes, color photographs/drawings contrary to the ink/black-and-white requirement may be construed as informal drawings so the application can get a filing date, but they are not permitted as formal drawings without a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the color photographs/drawings can be treated as formal drawings, applicant must submit a petition, the fee, the required statement in the specification, an explanation of why color is necessary, and three full sets of color photographs/drawings (inserted in bracketed examiner note). Use ¶ 15.45 guidance for handling informal color submissions and required followup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement drawing sheets and amendment procedure (37 CFR 1.121(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to an Office action to avoid abandonment; replacement sheets must follow specific content and labeling rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all figures appearing on the immediate prior version of that sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. Do not label a figure or figure number as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, remove it from the replacement sheet and, if necessary, renumber remaining figures and update the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. If all figures on a sheet are canceled, a replacement sheet is not required but present a marked-up copy labeled “Annotated Sheet” in the amendment or remarks explaining the change. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, notify applicant and inform of required corrective action in the next Office action. Use ¶ 15.05.04 wording and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling and presentation of annotated/canceled sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: When all figures on a drawing sheet are canceled, present a marked-up copy (labeled 'Annotated Sheet') showing that all figures on that drawing sheet have been canceled in the amendment or remarks explaining the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This annotated sheet should be included when all figures on a drawing sheet are canceled instead of submitting an empty replacement sheet. Ensure proper labeling and that the replacement/new sheets include the figures from the immediate prior version when applicable. Follow 37 CFR 1.121(d) labeling requirements and the examiner's instructions if changes are not accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing correction required prior to appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Any appeal of the design claim must include the correction of the drawings approved by the examiner (Ex parte Bevan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this requirement when there is an outstanding requirement for a drawing correction: the correction must be made and approved before filing an appeal; ¶ 15.05.05 form paragraph can be used in a FINAL rejection where drawing correction is outstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of new matter when amending or preparing new drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing new drawings in compliance with a requirement therefor, care must be exercised to avoid introduction of anything which could be construed to be new matter prohibited by 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 15.48 may be used to notify applicant of the necessity for good drawings. Addition of material (e.g., new broken-line boundaries other than straight broken lines, added surface shading that changes disclosure, or addition of features not present in the original) may be treated as new matter and is prohibited. Removal or addition of surface treatment must be evaluated to determine whether the underlying configuration was originally disclosed. Ensure antecedent support for any hatching/sectional additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity for clear, complete drawings (fatal if insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing or photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim and must be so clear and complete that nothing regarding the design sought to be patented is left to conjecture; an insufficient drawing may be fatal to validity under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize high quality execution as to clarity and completeness. An insufficient drawing may also negatively affect the effective filing date of a continuing application. Use form paragraph 15.48 and related MPEP guidance to notify applicants when drawings are inadequate and to require corrections or replacement sheets as appropriate.
